title: Harry Carney's baritone, stiff reed and playing seated
summary: Carney played baritone while Hardwick played bass sax when Bigard joined; he used a very stiff reed and played sitting because it was easier to manipulate.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: We were talking earlier about members of Duke's band and you mentioned something that was -- something I had never known before about Harry Carney. You said that when he was first playing the baritone sax? You said something about bass sax?
Bass sax.
Bass sax.
Uh-huh.
I didn't know he played bass sax.
When was that?
Oh, when I came in, when I got in the band he was.
He was playing bass sax?
No, he was playing baritone. Otto Hardwick was playing bass sax. That's what it was. I had it mixed up.
And you said that Harry used such a --
A stiff reed, a stiff reed, and then he had lumps all over his body. I used to ask him, 'Why do you use it?' And that's the only thing he could do.
To get the sound he wanted or to to play the horn at all?
No, to get what he wanted.
Did he always, then, stick with that same stiff reed all the way through?
Yeah, every time. Every time the reed goes dead and he'd put a new one, he's got to -- if it's not too stiff, he'd cut it. And that's the way he wanted it.
I know he always played sitting. He almost never played standing up. (Almost sitting down) Always standing up. Was
that the weight of the horn or was it his own personal preference?
No, that was because it was easier for him to manipulate, sitting down. You know, when you get used to a position and you try to change it, it's pretty hard, you know.
But he took so many of his solos sitting down.
Yeah.
